items_missed: Customer's name was not captured until minute twelve, and only because she asked for his. 'Okay. Okay. Well, what was your name?' is what finally triggered 'My name is Alex,' which then led into the profile creation. Eleven of the fifteen minutes — including the entire pricing block and both quoted totals — happened with no name, no email, and no lead record. If she had hung up after the $3,340 figure, this call produced nothing.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?' — the call went from 'how can I help?' straight to 'Were you looking for, for a move or did you also want to include like packing up of boxes as well?' She never got a roadmap or a timeframe for the call.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up.

Never asked about special considerations — long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns — on a move out of a two-story townhome with a garage, into a one-story house. Stair-to-door carry at a townhome is a real hours driver and it was never scoped.

Box count never established, on a full-pack quote. He told her 'the only thing that would be a separate charge would be for the actual boxes and packing materials themselves' and then never asked how many boxes that would be, never quoted a materials dollar figure, and never gave her a per-box or per-kit price. She has a 1,600 sq ft home being packed from scratch and zero visibility into the one line item he told her is extra.
Storage and additional stops never asked.
Access concerns never probed — no parking, no driveway, no truck access, no HOA at either address, on a townhome-to-house move.

Never asked the moving-stressor question. She volunteered plenty of texture — 'majority of it is trash can that we're not going to be taking with us,' 'I don't even own a kitchen table' — and none of it drew 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?'

No hourly rate was ever stated. Not once, in fifteen minutes. He quoted $3,340 and $3,564 as totals and mentioned 'two movers for a 48 hour day' (garbled in transcript), but the customer cannot back into a per-mover-per-hour number from anything he said. She is going to relay the total to her husband — 'so I can relay to my husband the 3000 the 3300 right' — with no rate behind it, which is the number he would want to interrogate.

Trip fee was raised and then abandoned. 'But we do charge trip fees depending on what zone that you would land on. So let me just go ahead and crunch what zip codes you have there, and then see if that applies to you or not.' He never came back to it. The customer does not know whether a trip fee is in her $3,340 or on top of it.

What's-included list was partial: 'moving blankets to stretch wrap to wrap it up any disassemble for stuff like bed frames, cribs mirrors on dresser.' No gas, no truck, no taxes, no insurance, no tools, no bands.
No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned — no $2,000, no 'repair, replace, or reimburse,' no 60¢/lb comparison. Zero insurance content on a $3,300 quote.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, on a two-day pack-and-move where the arrival window on day one determines whether day two works at all.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch. 'None of those things are separate charges' gestures at it, but the explicit no-credit-card-fee / no-fuel-surcharge / no-assembly-fee list never came — and he had a live opening because he'd just told her boxes and materials are the one thing that is extra.

Clock start was never explained and the 2.5 hour minimum was never mentioned. He covered fifteen-minute proration well — 'you would only be billed to the nearest fifteen minute increment of actual time used' — but never told her when the clock starts, when it stops, or that there is a floor underneath it.
No sense-check anywhere. The pricing block runs roughly 300 words and her entire contribution across it is 'Right.' and 'Okay. Okay.'

No typical time range for a 1,600 sq ft townhome. He anchored the whole estimate to an assumed full day on each of two days rather than to what homes this size actually take, which is the number she needed to judge whether the quote was sane.
Truck count never stated, and mover count only appeared embedded inside the assumption ('if you sent that two movers for a 48 hour day is probably overkill').
Stairs never factored into the estimate. She told him it is 'two bedroom or two floors. It's two floors,' and the two-story load never appeared in his hours reasoning.
Walk distance never asked at either address. No equivalents or plain-language anchors were used to make the hours concrete.

Zero booking attempt. He had a customer with three candidate date pairs (Oct 2-3 or 7-8), confirmed availability on all of them, and never once asked to hold any of them. The close was 'if you want like the progress of this conversation to be saved, what I can do for you is just get it all on an email for you' — a records-keeping offer, not a booking ask.

No deposit required was never mentioned. This is the miss that cost the most: she is taking a $3,340 number to her husband, and 'there is no deposit and no card on file, so I can hold October 7th right now and it costs you nothing' is the exact thing that keeps the date alive while they decide.

The email was framed as reply-with-questions, not reply-with-corrections: 'if you have any questions, if you want to upload any photos, whatever the case may be. You're welcome to just reply to that email with it.' No bolded-details framing, no ask to verify what he captured — which matters because he captured her scope loosely and is about to price it.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' and no business hours given.
top_strength: Alexander is the best consultative prober on the board this week, and the garage sequence is the proof. Most reps ask 'anything in the garage?' and write down yes. He asked 'just so I can kind of context realize that right now for your garage are you able to fit two vehicles inside that garage, or is it being occupied by a lot of inventory right now?' — a question designed to get a volume answer rather than a yes/no — and when she hedged he closed it out: 'it sounds like you're probably leaning more towards like, probably more minimal there in the garage as far as the inventory goes, is that right?' That is a rep actively de-scoping a job instead of letting ambiguity inflate it. He did the same on specialty items, naming the exclusion set so she knew what he was actually asking for: 'if you have any, any furniture that's gonna be particularly fragile or particularly heavy outside of the usual suspects of like a couch, or like a bed that we consider to just be like standard furniture.' His second real strength is proactive expectation-setting on the thing customers most often get blindsided by. He volunteered, unprompted, that a full pack roughly doubles the job and why: 'typically if we are doing the pack from scratch usually that's gonna double an estimate, because it requires the same amount of resources to fully consolidate a home, into boxes as, as the move itself.' Then he answered the same-day-pack-and-move question with a real threshold instead of a shrug — 'usually we only do that like a same day pack and move for up to about 900 square feet or so... once you start crossing through the 900 square foot, it generally becomes a little bit more untenable.' He also handled the sleep-here-tonight question with genuine reassurance ('whatever you needed us to leave unpacked for you... we would ask first before we start just wrapping up furniture') and the washer/dryer question with a clean scope line ('we can disconnect them to, that's not an extra charge. The only thing that we don't touch would be gas lines'). Every one of those is a question the customer would otherwise have taken to a competitor.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Alexander never said a rate. Fifteen minutes, two quoted totals, a full-pack explanation, and the customer cannot tell you what Einstein charges per hour. That is a structural problem, not an oversight — he builds estimates in his head and hands over the output, which means the customer has no way to sanity-check the number, no way to model 'what if it takes less time,' and nothing concrete to give the husband who is about to look at $3,340. The fix is a fixed opening to every pricing block: 'Pricing is super simple — it's a per-mover, per-hour rate. Wednesday and Thursday it's $X per mover, so a two-mover team is $Y an hour, and that includes the truck, gas, taxes, insurance, all the blankets and wrap, and all the disassembly and reassembly. The only separate charge is boxes and materials.' Rate first, then total. Second priority: he left two loops open that both cost money. He told her there is a trip fee, said he'd check her zips, and never said whether it applied — so the $3,340 has an unresolved fee floating next to it. And he built the whole estimate on a full eight-hour day per day while simultaneously telling her it might be overkill: 'if you sent that two movers for a 48 hour day is probably overkill then what I would probably recommend is just to send over some photos.' Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: quoting the high end and then verbally disowning it is the worst of both worlds — she banks the scary number and does not send the photos. He had already de-scoped this home with his own questions (minimal garage, no kitchen table, two light couches, nothing heavy or fragile, 1,600 sq ft) and had every reason to quote toward the middle and say so. This is the same conservative-padding pattern driving the 45-46% accuracy number, showing up in a rep whose probing was good enough to avoid it. Third: no booking attempt at all, on a customer who handed him three date pairs and asked him to check all of them. 'It looks like right now with you calling in advance. We still do have plenty of availability there' is the setup and he never took the swing. The line was: 'Since there's no deposit and nothing due until the move is done, let me pencil in Wednesday the 7th right now at no cost — it holds the crew, and if you and your husband land somewhere else you just tell me and I release it.' Fourth, the Save Your Ass speech barely registered. The only trace is 'just in case maybe you guys are able to get ahead of the packing and you no longer need it' — buried in a note about the email. On a call where the customer twice told him her garage is mostly trash she is not taking, the speech writes itself: 'Anything you can get out to the curb or into a carload before we get there comes straight off the clock — the loose stuff in drawers, the holiday tubs, the pictures off the walls. Does that make sense?' Finally: get the name in the first thirty seconds. He built a good profile at minute twelve; he should have built it at minute one, because everything before that point was unattributed work.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely conversational rather than scripted — he followed her down the garage tangent ('you know how these garages have those like little, like listed landings'), reassured her without being asked ('Oh, yeah, yeah, 100 percent. Yeah, whatever you needed us to leave unpacked for you'), and closed with real lightness ('Perfect, too easy' and 'I just wanna make sure it's nice'), which carried the customer to 'I appreciate it thank you so much'; held back from a 5 by zero use of her name and a 300-word pricing block that reduced her to 'Right. Okay. Okay.'
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace read is uncertain because the transcript garbles the single most load-bearing phrase on the call: 'a 48 hour day' appears three times where he almost certainly said 'a four to eight hour day,' and the same section produces 'a large credi say for piano' and 'to kinda like go the cleaning.' Audio is needed both to confirm the pacing judgment and to establish what hours assumption he actually gave the customer, since the whole estimate-accuracy read on this call turns on it.
